notes.text: Bengali skips the verb to be in the present. Ami chatro means I student, and that is a complete sentence.
Namaskar works for anyone. Muslim Bengalis often say salaam alaikum, and among friends it is just ki khobor: what news?
Three ways to say you: tui for childhood friends, tumi for equals, apni for respect. Get it wrong and people notice.
Your father's elder brother is jethu, his younger brother kaka. English says uncle and leaves you guessing.
Bhat kheyecho asks have you eaten rice, but it really means are you alright. Answer yes and someone relaxes.
Counting to a hundred means learning a hundred separate words. Ekattur is seventy-one, and no rule will help you guess it.
Tea without milk is called lal cha, red tea. Nobody thinks it looks red, but the name stuck.
Leaving someone, say ashchi, I am coming. Saying jachchi, I am going, sounds far too final for Bengali ears.
Kal means yesterday and tomorrow both. Only the verb tense tells you which, and porshu stretches two days either way.
Eggs and bananas are sold by the hali, a set of four. Ask for du hali and you carry home eight.
Nobody says I am ill. You say sharir kharap, body bad, as though the body were a separate troublesome thing.
Bari is the house, ghar a room inside it. Ask about someone's desher bari and you are asking about ancestry.
Kaj is job, chore and usefulness at once. Kaje lage means it comes in handy, literally it goes to work.
Feelings happen to you here. Amar bhalo lage is literally to me it feels good, never a plain I like it.
Bengalis say pujo, not puja. On the last day of Durga Pujo you greet everyone with Shubho Bijoya and sweets.
